title: Verification as Identity Accountability Personhood and the Scarcity of Verification in the Agent Economy
abstract: The Kaal Corpus argues that verification becomes the scarce input when agent intelligence is abundant and that deployer liability is the transitional rule for harm (Kaal 2026c, 2026g, 2026l). It states, in one sentence and by legal stipulation, that a persistent, non-transferable reputation record gives an agent an identity (Kaal 2026b, 2026l), but it does not develop the point. This Article develops it and adds what the corpus does not contain. It treats identity as a linkage rule that maps agent instances to records, shows that the rule’s error rates set the agent’s capacity to answer for harm, and states the minimal linkage at which an agent can answer for a given harm. It derives a model in which an agent holding such a record answers for harm from its own earnings and exit incentives, with the threshold standing at which a principal’s exposure falls to zero and two regimes of failure: a cliff, in which the agent exits and the injured party recovers nothing, and graceful degradation, in which the agent stays and pays what it can. It extends the model to strategic claimants, partial inheritance, correlated harm, an endogenous entry cost, verifier incentives and sponsorship chains, and it states the stake at which verifiers are honest, the places where the regress of verifiers ends, and the limits of sponsorship. It reports two registered tests of the decision rule, the first of which failed on a specification error that the Article corrects. It compares the record with existing agent-identity standards and reports a descriptive study of 1,156 feedback events in the ERC-8004 registries, which finds almost no evidence attached and no consequence. A documented search found no work that combines these elements. The evidence is limited. The tests use a prompted language model with no stake, the registry data cover one chain in one window, and the novelty search was not independent. Nature and scope of claims. This Article states a hypothesis about design opportunities. It makes no claim about the content of existing law, and it makes no normative claim about what any legal system should provide. Terms such as personhood, liability, principal and identity are used as design vocabulary. The propositions are conditional. The evidence for the underlying mechanisms is partial and is stated as such in Part VI.
